projects.name: Naturally Good
projects.desc: Took a wellness D2C brand from a quiet 2K audience to a 25K+ community with a real growth engine underneath — reporting straight to the founder, owning brand and performance as one.

blocks.title: The brand
blocks.text: Naturally Good is a health & wellness D2C brand — organic vegetables, honey, ghee, superfoods, seeds, teas and nutrition packs, backed by a farmer-first supply story. Great product, quietly under-marketed.

blocks.title: The challenge
blocks.text: A tiny 2K audience, brand awareness that didn't match product quality, rising acquisition costs, and no clear reason for a shopper to choose it over Country Delight, Two Brothers or the quick-commerce shelf.

blocks.title: My role
blocks.text: Brand Marketing Head, reporting to the founder. End-to-end owner: strategy, brand, content, performance, influencer, CRM, app growth and offline — the whole stack.

blocks.title: Objectives
items: Reposition the brand around a memorable, ownable story
Grow an engaged organic community, not a vanity following
Build a profitable performance engine at a defensible CAC
Launch and scale the app as a retention & subscription channel

blocks.title: Strategy
blocks.text: I repositioned Naturally Good from "another organic store" to a **farm-to-family wellness ritual** — anchoring every message in the farmer, the source and the health outcome. Then I built a content-and-influencer flywheel on top, and put a disciplined performance layer underneath so paid, organic and retention pulled in the same direction.

blocks.title: Execution
items: **Organic & social:** repositioned Instagram strategy, monthly content calendars, reels & story series, recipe and festival campaigns, healthy-lifestyle series, community games
**Farmer storytelling:** turned the supply chain into the brand's emotional core — farm events, apartment & lift activations, hyperlocal offline branding
**Performance:** Meta & Google Ads on ₹20L+/month, creative & funnel testing to cut CAC ~30% at 4.2× ROAS
**Influencer:** 50+ partnerships across 8 always-on channels, from nano food creators to wellness voices
**Commerce & retention:** Shopify D2C, Amazon listings & A+ content, quick-commerce presence (Zepto / Blinkit / BigBasket), WhatsApp & email flows, a subscription model and referral loops

**App:** launch strategy, download campaigns, Play Store optimization and referral drives to 15K+ installs with 22% Day-7 retention; prototyped an AI-powered family-nutrition app (Claude API) to deepen engagement and retention
**AI-embedded workflow:** generative AI (ChatGPT, Claude) woven into content, creative and campaign production to scale output without scaling headcount
**Packaging & decks:** packaging redesign and copy, plus marketing, sales & investor decks for the founder's office

blocks.title: Lessons
blocks.text: The story did the heavy lifting. Once the farmer-first narrative was clear, every channel got cheaper — creative resonated, influencers had something real to say, and retention followed because people bought into a belief, not a discount.

projects.name: CUPEESE
projects.desc: A cheesecake brand built from a blank page — name, identity, packaging, positioning and go-to-market — then launched to ₹8L+ in its first 90 days.

blocks.title: The idea
blocks.text: A premium, single-serve cheesecake worth talking about. No brand, no audience, no shelf — just a recipe and the conviction that dessert could be a small, repeatable ritual people fall in love with.

blocks.title: Naming & identity
blocks.text: I named it **CUPEESE** — cup + please, a little joyful, easy to say and own — and built the identity, logo and voice around indulgence you don't have to justify.

blocks.title: Positioning
blocks.text: Not "cheapest cake nearby" but the **small luxury you gift yourself**. Premium feel, honest ingredients, and packaging built to travel and to photograph.

blocks.title: Customer persona
blocks.text: Young urban indulgers and gifters — people who screenshot dessert, order for a friend's win, and repeat-buy when a brand makes them feel something. I designed the entire funnel around that emotional trigger.

blocks.title: Launch & growth
items: **Packaging & product:** designed the box, label copy and the unboxing moment as the first marketing asset
**Social & community:** built a 5,000+ community from zero with craveable content, story series and community campaigns
**Performance:** hyper-local paid campaigns tuned to delivery radius and repeat windows
**Commerce:** food-delivery aggregators plus WhatsApp commerce for direct, high-margin orders
**Retention & CRM:** loyalty and WhatsApp flows that drove 60% repeat purchase — the number I'm proudest of

blocks.title: Lessons
blocks.text: In food, repeat is the whole game. Getting the first order is marketing; getting the second is the brand. Packaging, community and CRM did more for LTV than any single ad ever did.

projects.name: HIOC · Arry Foods
projects.desc: Turned organic search into a real acquisition channel for a food brand — cutting reliance on paid while growing traffic and rankings, on an ₹18L+ budget.

blocks.title: The challenge
blocks.text: A food brand leaning too hard on paid, with thin organic visibility and rising costs. The job: build durable, compounding demand that didn't reset to zero the moment ad spend paused.

blocks.title: Strategy
blocks.text: Treat SEO and content as a **flywheel**, not a checkbox. Own the searches customers actually make, build community and CRM to keep them, and let organic quietly take load off the paid budget.

blocks.title: My role
blocks.text: Brand & marketing strategy across the food business — SEO, content, community, CRM and budget across social, WhatsApp commerce and food-aggregator channels.

blocks.title: Execution
items: **SEO & content:** keyword strategy, on-page and blogs targeting real buyer intent — 15+ keywords to page one
**Google ranking:** grew organic traffic ~120% and reduced paid dependency ~40%
**Community & CRM:** built retention loops and loyalty to lift repeat and lifetime value
**Budget:** managed ₹18L+ across social, WhatsApp commerce and aggregators with positive ROI

blocks.title: Lessons
blocks.text: Paid rents attention; organic owns it. The brands that win in food are the ones that build a demand base they don't have to re-buy every month.

projects.name: Exotic Learning
projects.desc: Where it started: a growth-and-conversion funnel that turned 1,000+ leads into 90 placements — proof that the fundamentals of demand are the same, whatever you're selling.

blocks.title: The challenge
blocks.text: Fill 15+ roles fast, from a cold start, with no established pipeline — and do it efficiently enough that the funnel could scale.

blocks.title: Approach
blocks.text: I ran recruitment like a growth campaign: sourced and nurtured candidates as an audience, built conversion into every stage, and optimized the funnel on real numbers.

blocks.title: Result
blocks.text: 1,000+ leads into 90 placements (9% conversion) across 15+ roles in three months, a 10K+ candidate pipeline, and time-to-fill cut ~20%.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.text: This is the foundation everything else is built on. Whether the "product" is a job, a cheesecake or a jar of ghee, the discipline is identical: understand the audience, build a funnel, measure honestly, and improve the number that matters.

posts.title: Wellness reel series
posts.subtitle: From Farm to Wellness How I Turned Educational Content into a Brand-Building Strategy for Naturally Good

meta.label: Objective
meta.value: Build trust, educate consumers, and position Naturally Good as a wellness-first organic brand through educational short-form content.

body.text: The Challenge

When I joined Naturally Good, I noticed that most organic brands were communicating in the same way—posting product images, talking about discounts, or simply highlighting that their vegetables were "100% organic." The problem was that consumers weren't looking for vegetables; they were looking for better health, safe food for their families, and brands they could trust. At the same time, there was a significant knowledge gap. Many people didn't know:

items: The difference between fresh farm produce and stored vegetables
The nutritional benefits of everyday vegetables
How food choices directly impact long-term health

body.text: I believed that if we could educate people instead of constantly selling to them, we could build stronger relationships and create a brand people genuinely trusted.
The Insight
People don't connect emotionally with vegetables. They connect with:
Instead of asking people to buy from Naturally Good, I wanted to give them a reason to believe in the brand first.
The Strategy

I created a recurring Farm Education & Wellness Reel Series that combined educational storytelling with authentic farm experiences. Rather than focusing on products, every reel answered a question or solved a problem. The content revolved around three simple themes: 🌱 Know Your Food Helping consumers understand where their vegetables come from, how they're grown, and why farming practices matter.
Eat Better

Educating people about seasonal vegetables, nutrition, healthy habits, and the benefits of eating fresh, chemical-free produce. See the Difference Using real farm footage to showcase harvesting, sorting, packaging, and the journey from farm to home, making transparency a key part of the brand experience.
Content Framework
Every reel followed a simple storytelling structure that kept the content informative and engaging. 1. Hook Capture attention within the first few seconds. Examples:

items: "Did you know spinach starts losing nutrients soon after harvest?"
"You're eating vegetables every day—but are they actually fresh?"

body.text: 2. Educate Break down one concept into simple, easy-to-understand information using relatable language and visuals. Topics included:

3. Show, Don't Tell Instead of relying on stock visuals, we filmed directly on the farm—harvesting vegetables, preparing orders, and showcasing the people behind the produce. This made the content more authentic and trustworthy. 4. Soft Brand Integration Rather than ending with "Buy Now," the content naturally connected the learning back to Naturally Good's mission of delivering fresh, organically grown vegetables.
My Role
I managed the campaign from ideation to execution. This included:

Continuously refining the content strategy based on performance

body.text: Marketing Principles Behind the Campaign

1. Education Before Promotion Instead of selling products directly, we focused on sharing useful knowledge. This helped Naturally Good become a trusted source of information rather than just another organic food brand.
2. Storytelling Builds Trust Showing real farms, real harvesting, and real people created authenticity that polished advertisements often lack. People trust what they can see.

3. Value-First Content Every reel was designed to teach something practical. If viewers learned something new—even without making a purchase—the content had achieved its purpose. This encouraged more saves, shares, and repeat engagement.
4. Emotional Marketing We shifted the conversation from vegetables to outcomes that mattered:
People relate more to the benefits of healthy living than to the product itself.

5. Consistency Creates Authority By consistently publishing educational content, Naturally Good strengthened its identity as a reliable voice in organic farming and wellness, making the brand more memorable over time.

By combining farm education with wellness storytelling, I transformed social media into a platform that informed, inspired, and built trust. The result was a stronger brand identity, deeper audience engagement, and a content strategy that supported long-term business growth.

posts.title: Ghee & honey range

body.text: Packaging Innovation
Designing Packaging That Added Value Beyond the

Product While developing the packaging for Naturally Good's Pure Raw Honey and A2 Bilona Cow Ghee, I wanted the customer experience to begin the moment they opened the package. Instead of treating the packaging as just a container, I looked for small improvements that could make the products more convenient and enjoyable to use every day.
The Challenge

Premium food products are often differentiated through ingredients and branding, but many brands overlook what happens after the customer receives the product. I asked a simple question: "How can the packaging continue to serve the customer even after the purchase?" The goal was to make the experience feel thoughtful, practical, and premium without adding unnecessary complexity.
The Solution

🍯 Honey – Complimentary Wooden Honey Dipper One common challenge with honey is pouring or serving it without creating a mess. To solve this, I introduced a complimentary wooden honey dipper inside every honey package. This small addition allowed customers to:

items: Use the product exactly as intended

body.text: Beyond functionality, the wooden dipper complemented the natural and artisanal positioning of the brand, making the packaging feel more complete and gift-worthy.
🫙 A2 Bilona Cow Ghee – Wooden Spoon

For the A2 Bilona Cow Ghee range, I introduced a premium wooden spoon with every jar. Customers often use regular kitchen spoons, which may be wet or unsuitable for repeatedly handling ghee. Including a dedicated wooden spoon helped:

items: Encourage customers to use the product with a dedicated utensil
Create a more thoughtful unboxing experience

body.text: It transformed a simple purchase into a more complete product experience.
My Role
I was responsible for identifying these customer experience opportunities and integrating them into the packaging strategy.
My involvement included:

items: Ensuring the accessories complemented the packaging design
Aligning the additions with the brand's premium positioning

body.text: Marketing Principles Applied
Customer-Centric Design
The packaging was designed around how customers actually use the product, making everyday interactions easier and more enjoyable.
Value-Added Packaging
Instead of competing only on price, the product delivered additional value through useful accessories that enhanced the overall experience.
Experience Marketing
The unboxing experience became part of the brand story. Customers didn't just receive honey or ghee—they received thoughtfully designed products that reflected Naturally Good's attention to detail.
Premium Positioning
Small details often shape perceptions of quality. The wooden dipper and spoon elevated the products, helping justify their premium positioning while creating a memorable first impression.
Brand Differentiation
These additions created a clear point of difference from competing products that offered similar ingredients but overlooked the customer experience.
Business Impact
These packaging enhancements helped Naturally Good strengthen its premium positioning by making the products more functional and memorable. The initiative contributed to:

items: Better product usability in everyday life
Higher customer satisfaction through thoughtful design
Improved differentiation in a competitive category

body.text: Most importantly, these were not expensive additions—they were meaningful ones. A simple wooden honey dipper and a dedicated ghee spoon transformed the products from everyday pantry items into thoughtfully designed experiences.

posts.takeaway: Great packaging doesn't end when the customer opens the box—it continues every time they use the product. By introducing a complimentary wooden honey dipper with our Pure Raw Honey and a dedicated wooden spoon with our A2 Bilona Cow Ghee, I transformed functional packaging into a customer experience. These small but intentional innovations improved usability, reinforced our premium positioning, and demonstrated that thoughtful design can create lasting brand value without increasing complexity.

posts.title: How I launched a brand from zero
posts.subtitle: The unglamorous first 90 days — name, package, first customer, first repeat. Notes from taking CUPEESE from a blank page to real revenue.
posts.excerpt: The unglamorous first 90 days — name, package, first customer, first repeat.

body.text: There was no brand. Just a category problem.

When I started on CUPEESE, there was no logo, no name, no packaging — just a premium cheesecake product that looked, on paper, like every other dessert brand in a crowded category. Cakes, pastries and cheesecakes all tend to look the same on a shelf or a delivery app. Before I could think about a single creative asset, I had to solve a category problem: what would make someone remember this dessert five minutes after they finished it?
The idea came before the identity

Instead of starting with a logo, I started with the product experience. Traditional cheesecake slices need a plate, cutlery, careful handling — none of which survives a delivery bag or a work-from-café afternoon. That observation became the whole brand: “Cheesecake in a Cup.” A transparent cup that showed off the layers, was easy to carry, easy to eat one-handed, and looked good on a phone screen before it was ever tasted. The packaging wasn't decoration on top of the product — it was the product.
Naming, identity, and the discipline of "no"

CUPEESE — cup + please — had to do a lot of work in one word: playful, easy to say, easy to own. Every decision after that, from the colour palette to the outer box, got tested against one question: does this feel indulgent without feeling like it's trying too hard? A lot of good ideas got cut because they answered a different brief than the one the brand actually needed.
Shipping before it felt ready

0→1 doesn't reward perfectionism. I took the concept through naming, identity, packaging and positioning, then ran the actual launch — pricing, channel selection, the first batch of creative, the first cohort of customers. There wasn't a big-budget campaign behind it. There was a product people wanted to photograph, a story that was easy to repeat, and a go-to-market plan sized to the brand's actual stage, not an aspirational one.
What ₹8L+ in 90 days actually taught me

The brand crossed ₹8L+ in its first 90 days, but the number that mattered more to me was repeat orders — proof that people weren't just buying the novelty once. Building something from zero means every early customer is also market research. I watched what people actually said about the cup format, not what I assumed they'd say, and used that to sharpen the packaging copy and the reorder messaging in the following weeks.

posts.takeaway: Launching from zero isn't about having more resources than the category leaders — it's about being more specific than they are. CUPEESE won its first ninety days by being unmistakably itself, not by being louder.

posts.title: Why storytelling beats advertising
posts.subtitle: A sharp story is the cheapest, most durable growth lever you'll ever build. What a farm-education reel series taught me about earning attention instead of buying it.
posts.excerpt: A sharp story is the cheapest, most durable growth lever you'll ever build.

body.text: Everyone was saying the same thing

When I joined Naturally Good, most organic brands — including us, at the time — were communicating the same way: product photos, discount codes, and a claim of “100% organic” that had stopped meaning anything to anyone. Customers weren't actually shopping for vegetables. They were shopping for better health, safer food for their families, and a brand they could trust. That gap between what we were saying and what people were actually looking for was the whole opportunity.
People don’t connect with a product. They connect with an outcome.

Nobody feels strongly about a carrot. They feel strongly about better immunity, a healthier family, transparency about where their food comes from. So instead of asking people to buy from us, I built a recurring Farm Education & Wellness Reel Series designed to give people a reason to believe in the brand before they were ever asked to purchase anything. Every reel answered a real question — why seasonal produce matters, what the difference is between fresh and stored vegetables — instead of pushing a product.
Show, don’t sell

We filmed directly on the farm: harvesting, sorting, packaging, the people behind the produce. No stock footage, no studio gloss. Real footage of a real supply chain is a kind of storytelling advertising can't fake — it's evidence, not a claim. Every reel closed with what I called soft brand integration: never “Buy Now,” always a quiet connection back to the brand's actual mission.
The compounding effect of teaching instead of selling

Education-first content does something paid advertising structurally can't: it gets saved, shared, and rewatched, because it's useful independent of the purchase decision. Over time, that consistency did more than move a single campaign metric — it repositioned Naturally Good from “another organic brand” to a trusted source of information on food and wellness, which is a much harder position for competitors to copy.

posts.takeaway: Advertising rents attention. Storytelling earns trust, and trust is the only thing that compounds. If viewers walked away having learned something real, the content had already done its job — the sale was a natural next step, not the pitch.

posts.title: Building D2C brands in India
posts.subtitle: What actually works when quick-commerce, CAC and a genuinely offline-first customer reshape the funnel — lessons from running lift media, society activations and lifecycle journeys on the ground.
posts.excerpt: What actually works when quick-commerce and CAC reshape the funnel.

body.text: The funnel doesn’t start online here

A lot of D2C playbooks assume the customer's first touchpoint is a scroll-stopping ad. For a subscription organic brand like Naturally Good, that assumption breaks fast — the target customer is a health-conscious family in a premium residential society, and digital ads alone weren't creating the local presence or trust that a recurring farm-to-home subscription needs. The insight that changed the strategy: our ideal customers spend a few uninterrupted seconds in an apartment lift every single day, and that's a moment worth owning.
Hyperlocal beats broad, every time

I planned and executed a lift media campaign across premium societies in Gurgaon, eventually overseeing the installation of more than 500 lift posters. The objective wasn't reach for its own sake — it was consistent, repeated exposure within a tightly defined neighbourhood, so residents saw the brand daily until it stopped feeling like advertising and started feeling like a fact about the building they lived in.
Stack the channels, don’t rotate them

Lift posters alone aren't a strategy — they're one layer. I combined lift media with apartment activations and door-to-door sampling inside the same societies, building a connected 360° journey instead of three disconnected tactics: awareness in the lift, a tactile product experience at the activation, and a direct conversation with a sampling team at the door. Each layer made the next one convert better, because the resident had already half-recognised the brand before the human conversation even started.
Different customers need different lifecycles

Running lifecycle marketing across two very different businesses — HIOC, a café where decisions are impulsive, and Naturally Good, a subscription that needs trust and reassurance before a customer commits — taught me lifecycle marketing is never one-size-fits-all. A café customer needs a great first visit and a reason to come back this week. A subscription customer needs education, proof, and a slow build of confidence before the first order, let alone the fifth.
You can’t manage what you can’t see in one place

With activity spread across Meta, Google, WhatsApp, offline activations, Amazon and a sales team, no single platform's report could answer basic questions like which channel actually drove the best leads. Building centralized growth dashboards across three brands was what made offline and online marketing comparable on the same terms, and what let us reallocate budget toward what was actually working instead of what was easiest to measure.

posts.takeaway: D2C in India rewards brands that treat offline and online as one connected system, not two separate budgets. The lift poster, the sampling table and the retention email all have to tell the same story, in the order the customer actually experiences them.

posts.title: The future of organic branding
posts.subtitle: Turning the farmer and the source into the strongest asset you own — what building farm experiences and educational content taught me about where organic brands need to go next.
posts.excerpt: Turning the farmer and the source into the strongest asset you own.

body.text: Claims are cheap. Proof isn’t.

Every organic brand says “100% organic.” It's on every pack, every ad, every landing page, and it has stopped persuading anyone. The next stage for organic branding isn't a better version of that claim — it's replacing the claim with evidence the customer can actually see, touch, or visit.
Let people walk the farm

We turned Naturally Good's own farms into a brand experience through Farm to Family events, inviting customers to harvest vegetables themselves, walk the fields, and meet the people growing their food. That kind of transparency does something a certification logo can't: it makes trust a lived experience instead of a printed claim, and it turns customers into advocates who've genuinely seen the supply chain rather than been told about it.
Education is the new packaging

Alongside the farm visits, a recurring wellness reel series answered the questions customers actually had — why seasonal produce matters, how food choices affect long-term health — using real farm footage instead of stock visuals. The brands that will win the next decade of organic aren't the ones with the cleanest packaging copy; they're the ones that treat customer education as a core product, not a marketing afterthought.
The source is the story

Whether it was a wooden honey dipper that made the sourcing of raw honey tangible, or a farm walkthrough that let a family see exactly where their vegetables came from, the pattern was the same: the most persuasive asset an organic brand owns isn't its logo, it's its actual origin. Brands that invest in making that origin visible — through events, content, and packaging that carries the story forward past the point of purchase — build a kind of trust performance marketing alone can't buy.

posts.takeaway: The future of organic branding is less about louder claims and more about shorter distance between the customer and the source. Show the farm. Let people taste the difference. The rest of the brand follows from that.

posts.title: Marketing lessons from FMCG
posts.subtitle: What selling honey, ghee, superfoods and cheesecake across three very different brands taught me about repeat purchase, retention, and creative that actually converts.
posts.excerpt: What selling honey and cheesecake taught me about repeat and retention.

body.text: Packaging doesn’t end at the unboxing

Premium food products are usually differentiated through ingredients and branding, but most brands stop thinking about packaging the moment the box is opened. When we developed packaging for Naturally Good's Pure Raw Honey and A2 Bilona Cow Ghee, we added a complimentary wooden honey dipper and a dedicated wooden spoon — small additions that solved a real usage problem and meant the packaging kept adding value every single time the customer used the product, not just once at unboxing.
A new range needs an ecosystem, not just new SKUs

Launching the Superfoods range taught me that a product launch isn't really about the product — it's about making a shelf full of new SKUs feel like they already belong to the brand family. Every product had to look and feel consistent, and go-to-market had to be integrated across packaging, product photography, Amazon listings, website content and social, rather than treating each new item as its own mini-launch.
One creative strategy doesn’t work across brands

Running performance creative across three brands in the same food and beverage category — Naturally Good, HIOC and Cupeese — made it obvious that customers buy the same category for completely different reasons. A Naturally Good customer is investing in long-term health through a subscription. An HIOC customer is making a spontaneous, craving-driven café decision. A Cupeese customer is buying indulgence, celebration, or a gift. Copying one brand's ad formula onto another's audience is the fastest way to waste a media budget.
Retention is a design decision, not a follow-up email

Across FMCG and D2C alike, the products that earned repeat purchase were the ones where retention was designed in from the packaging stage — a reason to keep the container, a reason to reorder, a small delight that made the second purchase easier to justify than the first. Growth dashboards across all three brands made this visible: the campaigns that looked good on reach were rarely the ones that moved repeat-purchase rate, and the packaging-level decisions often outperformed the media-level ones.

posts.takeaway: FMCG rewards brands that treat every touchpoint — the packaging, the ad, the follow-up message — as part of one connected customer relationship, not as separate line items on a media plan.
